course.learn: Encryption can be applied at different levels of granularity: full disk, partition, volume, file, database, or individual record/field. The best level depends on what threats and workflows must be protected.
course.why: Broader encryption is easier to deploy consistently, while fine-grained encryption can protect selected sensitive data even from other parts of the system.
course.example: A laptop uses full-disk encryption for theft protection, while a database also encrypts a sensitive customer identifier at the field level.
course.exam: Choose the encryption layer that matches the threat: stolen device often favors full-disk; protecting selected database values may require field/record-level encryption.

slides.title: Types
slides.teach: Focus on the differences between the listed types and the clue words that distinguish them in exam questions.

course.learn: This section focuses on **Types** within **Encryption**. Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand the data. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret; asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair.
course.why: Encryption is one of the primary ways to protect confidentiality for data at rest and in transit.
course.example: A laptop uses full-disk encryption, while a TLS session protects web traffic crossing an untrusted network.
course.exam: Encryption = confidentiality and reversible with the correct key. Hashing is one-way and primarily supports integrity.

slides.title: Key Exchange
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Cryptographic strength depends on using the correct key type, algorithm, key length, and exchange method. Keys must be generated, distributed, stored, rotated, and retired securely.
course.why: A strong algorithm can still fail if keys are weak, exposed, reused too long, or exchanged insecurely.
course.example: A server uses asymmetric cryptography to establish trust and exchange key material, then switches to fast symmetric encryption for the session.
course.exam: Focus on purpose: symmetric = fast shared secret; asymmetric = public/private pair; longer keys generally increase brute-force difficulty but algorithm choice also matters.
